text.headline: Achi Church: A Medieval Gem
text.text:
Located on the right bank of the Achi River, on an artificially raised hill, this small hall-type church is constructed from neatly dressed, regular square-cut stone blocks. The church features carved crosses above its western and southern entrances, with a five-line inscription in asomtavruli script above the southern doorway. The eastern façade boasts refined stone carving considered among the finest in Guria. Modern art-historical research dates Achi Church to the late thirteenth century, highlighting its architectural and decorative significance. Beyond its aesthetic value, Achi Church holds a crucial historical ecclesiastical function.

text.headline: Georgian Polyphony
text.text:
Georgian polyphonic music, a rich tradition recognised by UNESCO for its intricate counterpoint and unique techniques such as Krimanchuli in Guria and ornamented upper voices in Kakheti, is deeply intertwined with the daily life of Georgians. This musical heritage accompanies communal labour, social settings, work, feasting, and rituals, serving as a cultural glue that binds communities together during various activities. The tradition is rooted in Georgia’s unique position between East and West, characterised by complex vocal textures and strong regional identities.
The region of Guria in western Georgia exemplifies this tradition with its intricate counterpoint and high degree of independence between vocal lines. This region is also known for rare examples of four-part vocal polyphony, particularly within certain work-song repertoires.
In contrast, Kakheti in eastern Georgia features polyphonic singing that accompanies work, feasting, and ritual practices but follows a different vocal approach. Many songs in this region feature heavily ornamented upper voices supported by a sustained drone bass, creating a dense sonic foundation while allowing for variation across genres and performance contexts.

text.headline: Gremi Church of the Archangels
text.text:
The Gremi Church of the Archangels, located in the Gremi citadel in the region of Kakheti, is another significant monument within this tradition, dating from 1565 and built on the orders of King Levan of Kakheti. This church served both religious and royal functions, with the southern arm used as a royal section where King Levan attended services and was subsequently buried. The church was extensively damaged during Shah Abbas I’s campaigns of 1614–1616, resulting in the loss of its political and economic significance in Kakheti.

text.headline: Gremi Church: Fragmented Frescoes
text.text:
The original fresco ensemble of the Gremi Church has not survived intact. Part of the painting was lost during restoration in the seventeenth century, with many scenes and figures surviving only in fragments. The fresco program includes biblical scenes, individual saints, Church Fathers, martyrs, and saints associated with Christian hymnography. The cycle of the Great Feasts begins with the Annunciation and ends with the Dormition of the Virgin. Fragments of representations of the Virgin and the Archangels, as well as scenes associated with Holy Communion, survive in the sanctuary. Much of the dome painting has been lost; however, based on surviving fragments, it is believed that the central dome originally depicted Christ Pantocrator. The fresco decoration of the church was executed by two monks from Thessaloniki - Chartualrios and Protosynkellos. The frescoes at Gremi Church showcase a blend of artistic traditions from Mount Athos and the wider post-Byzantine Orthodox world, combined with local Georgian elements.

ev1794310083088.title: Shemokmedi chanters
ev1794310083088.description:
The chant tradition of Shemokmedi becomes particularly well documented around the turn of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. One of its most prominent representatives was Anton Dumbadze (1824–1907), a Shemokmedi chanter who played a key role in the revival and consolidation of Gurian church chant. His pupil was Melkisedek Nakashidze, while Nakashidze’s pupil, Artem Erkomaišvili, preserved the chants of the Shemokmedi school through live performance in the twentieth century. More than one hundred chants from the Shemokmedi school are preserved in recordings of Artem Erkomaišvili’s performances.
The Shemokmedi chant tradition is also associated with Varlam Simonishvili (1884–1950), a singer and chanter. From 1901, he worked with Filimon Koridze as a teacher of chant and later also took part in the recording of chants. Simonishvili is buried in the vicinity of Shemokmedi Monastery.

text.headline: Achi Church: Tradition
text.text:
Historically, Achi Church was dedicated to St George and served as an important ecclesiastical centre. The feast of St George at Achi was traditionally celebrated in November, with rituals connected to the church’s painted decoration. Today, Achi Church remains an active place of worship and is home to a convent dedicated to the Iveria Icon of the Most Holy Mother of God, where nuns live according to monastic rule.

ev1794312977140.title: Achi Church Frescos
ev1794312977140.description:
The frescoes within Achi Church are another remarkable feature, dating back to the late thirteenth century. These paintings exhibit a high level of artistic accomplishment and belong to a group of monuments known for their exceptional quality. The overall colour palette includes gold, green, and soft pearly tones, with faces rendered in a manner reminiscent of Byzantine monuments from the early Palaeologan period. Despite these influences, the frescoes clearly continue established Georgian iconographic traditions.
One distinctive feature is the iconographic treatment of St George's cycle, which includes unique scenes such as the saint defeating the dragon and rescuing a maiden, not commonly found in Georgian or Byzantine monumental painting.
The Achi frescoes also show artistic parallels with those of Trabzon, particularly those of Hagia Sophia. These similarities are likely due to historical connections between Trabzon and Guria. However, the style and figure types remain firmly rooted in local Georgian artistic traditions. The names of the artists who painted these frescoes are not known with certainty, but it is believed that a Georgian artist well-versed in Byzantine art created them.

ev1794319190337.title: Achi Church: History and Legend
ev1794319190337.description: Achi was one of the important ecclesiastical centres of Guria, where Gurian princes took particular care of the church. One notable artefact associated with Achi is a silver cross covered with gold, documented by Ekvtime Taqaishvili in 1907. This cross bears an asomtavruli inscription linking it to the reign of Queen Tamar (1184–1212). Local legends add to the church's mystique, including a tradition about a devi (ogre/demon) that terrorised the village until St George killed it and turned it to stone, leading to the construction of Achi Church in honour of the saint. Another legend suggests that pigeons laid down a trail of wood chips, guiding the choice of the church's site.

ev1794311065884.title: Shemokmedi: the Transfer of the Icon of the Transfiguration from Zarzma to Guria
ev1794311065884.description: An important episode in the history of Shemokmedi is connected with Samtskhe-Saatabago. Drawing on a charter of Vakhtang Gurieli, Bakradze describes the transfer of an icon from Zarzma to Guria following the devastation of Zarzma, and the construction at Shemokmedi of a church dedicated to the icon. In his account of the antiquities of Shemokmedi, Ekvtime Takaishvili notes that the first description by Bakradze had omitted the icon of the Transfiguration, which had been brought from Zarzma and was kept in the Church of Zarzma at Shemokmedi. According to Takaishvili, the inscription beneath the icon bears the date 886, indicating its antiquity and making it one of the oldest icons associated with Guria known at the time (Takaishvili 1907: 37–38).

ev1794301636441.title: Shemokmedi: the architectural complex
ev1794301636441.description: The monastery is located on the left bank of the Bzhuzhi River, on a low hill in the village of Shemokmedi. The complex consists of two interconnected churches: the domeless Church of the Saviour and the domed Church of the Transfiguration, also known as the Church of Zarzma. In the nineteenth century, Dimitri Bakradze personally studied Shemokmedi and provided a detailed description of its architecture, frescoes, inscriptions and ecclesiastical antiquities. He considered Shemokmedi one of the richest churches and monasteries in Guria and noted that it housed valuable ecclesiastical objects brought from different parts of Georgia, particularly from Samtskhe-Saatabago (Bakradze 1987).

text.headline: Shemokmedi: Georgian Sacred Chant Heritage
text.text:
The particular importance of Shemokmedi is also evident in the history of Georgian sacred chant. The monastery was an important historical centre for the transmission of Georgian church chant from one generation to another. Among the earliest known figures associated with the Shemokmedi school are Mate Gogitidze, abbot of Shemokmedi, and his nephew Ioane Gogitidze, who is described in the sources as a mg̣alobeli (chanter) (Bakradze 1987). Several neumed chant collections from Shemokmedi Monastery have also survived and are now preserved at the National Centre of Manuscripts. Together, these sources provide written evidence of the monastery’s centuries-old chant tradition.
